item.title: The Long Read: What A Synced Post Looks Like
item.description: A post long enough to earn a progress bar and a table of contents, so the heading ids have something to anchor.
item.dc:creator: Fixture Author
item.content:encoded:
Every publishing system eventually has to answer the same question twice: where does a post live, and who decides how it looks. The answer this site gives is that the post can live anywhere and the look is never negotiable, which is a stricter position than it first sounds.

A feed hands you markup somebody else wrote, and that markup arrives carrying opinions. It has classes naming a design system you do not use, inline styles pinned to a column width you do not have, and wrapper elements whose only job is to hold those two things. None of it survives the trip.

The typography is not up for negotiation

Strip the attributes and what is left is a document: paragraphs, headings, lists, quotes, tables, figures. Those are exactly the elements the article stylesheet already has rules for, written for the hand-authored posts that came first. A synced post inherits them by having nothing of its own to say.

That is the whole trick, and it is a subtraction rather than an addition. There is no translation layer mapping a foreign class onto a local one, no per-publication stylesheet, no list of overrides that has to grow every time the upstream editor ships a new block type. An element either survives sanitization or it does not.

The failure mode this avoids is the interesting one. A translation layer looks fine on the day it is written and rots quietly afterwards, because it fails open: an unmapped class renders as unstyled content that still looks approximately right, and nobody notices until a reader mentions that one post looks strange.

The layout is controlled entirely by the site's existing components. Anything else is an import of somebody else's design system by accident.

Dropping the wrapper elements is the part that feels aggressive and is not. A container carrying no class and no style carries no information at all, so keeping it would preserve the shape of a layout whose rules have already been deleted.

What survives, and why the list is short

The allowlist is data rather than code, and it is small on purpose. Five elements may carry attributes; everything else reaches the page bare. Links keep their destination and gain the attributes an outbound link should have. Images keep their source, their dimensions and their alternative text.

  • Paragraphs, headings and horizontal rules, unadorned.
  • Lists, ordered and otherwise, nested as deeply as the author nested them.
  • Quotes, figures and captions, which is most of what an essay is made of.
  • Tables, because a table that loses its structure loses its meaning.

Embedded frames are the exception that proves the rule. An iframe is not content, it is a second document with its own scripts and its own network access, and no amount of attribute filtering makes that safe. Each one becomes a labelled link and is counted, so the count can be read later.

ElementKeptNote
ayeshref, title; rel and target are forced
imgyesdropped entirely if the source is not absolute
iframenoreplaced by a labelled link
divnochildren kept, wrapper discarded

Reading time has to agree with itself

Two posts of the same length must report the same number of minutes, or the number is worse than useless — it is confidently wrong. That sounds trivial until the two posts arrive by different routes: one counted from a syntax tree at build time, the other from stored markup at request time.

The constant and the rounding therefore live in one module and both counters call it. What each counter excludes has to match too. A fenced block is not prose, so the tree walk skips it, and the markup counter drops the same elements whole rather than merely stripping their tags.

const minutes = Math.max(1, Math.round(words / 200));

Entities are the other half. Markup that has been through a serializer says you're where the author typed an apostrophe, and a naive split on whitespace counts that as one word only if the entity has been decoded first. Get it wrong and every post with dialogue in it reads long.

Anchors are a rendering detail with teeth

A table of contents is generated from the headings on the page, and it links to them by identifier. Hand-authored posts get those identifiers from a component that renders each heading, which works precisely because a component renders it. Injected markup never passes through that component.

So the identifiers are added earlier, before the markup is handed to anything that renders. They have to be unique, because the list keys on them and two identical ones is a collision, and they have to be non-empty, because an empty one is a link that goes nowhere and a key that is shared.

Both edge cases are real rather than theoretical. Essays repeat headings — two sections called "What changed" in a year-in-review is ordinary — and a heading made entirely of punctuation reduces to nothing at all once it has been through a slugifier that keeps only letters and numbers.

None of this is visible when it works. That is the argument for checking it against a rendered page rather than against a function: the failure is a table of contents that looks right and does nothing, which is exactly the kind of thing a unit test written by the same person who wrote the bug will happily confirm.
